content: When a child is upset, it is important to help them calm themselves. Similarly, patience is essential when they are learning a new skill. Encouraging happiness in the child and fostering an environment where they can make others happy is equally important. For example, a caregiver assisting a child in stacking cups of different sizes helps the child develop several skills, including physical (motor) skills, social skills, cognitive skills, and emotional skills. To promote child development, it is crucial to focus on the care the child receives rather than solely on what they can or should do at a particular age. Recommendations for play and communication activities are designed to help families stimulate the child’s development. These activities evolve and become more complex as the child grows older, providing opportunities for the child to learn new skills at different stages of development. For instance, the recommendations outlined in the Counseling Cards provide age-specific guidance for play and communication activities, which also help families learn how to care for their child effectively. From birth, caregivers should engage in play and communication with their child. This interaction helps caregivers become sensitive to the child’s needs and respond appropriately to their attempts to communicate. Sensitivity and responsiveness are fundamental caregiving skills that enable parents and other caregivers to provide better care, contributing to the child’s survival, healthy growth, and development. A sensitive caregiver recognizes the child’s signals, such as hunger, discomfort, or affection, and responds immediately and appropriately. For example, a caregiver who notices signs of hunger in a child, such as fussiness or sucking on their hand, can feed the child before they start crying. Similarly, a responsive caregiver acts quickly to protect the child from danger or provide comfort when the child is distressed. Caregivers should also be aware of the child’s developmental needs at different ages. For newborns (birth to 1 week), play involves allowing the baby to see, hear, feel, and move freely. Caregivers should avoid covering the baby’s face for long periods and should not swaddle the baby tightly for extended durations, as this restricts movement and exploration. Instead, caregivers can hold the baby close, gently stroke their skin, and soothe them when upset. Communication with newborns involves looking into their eyes, smiling, and talking to them, which helps the baby learn to communicate and trust that their needs will be met. For infants aged 1 week to 6 months, play activities include encouraging the child to reach for and grab objects, follow moving items with their eyes, and explore textures and sensations by putting safe objects in their mouth. Communication at this stage involves responding to the child’s sounds, copying their vocalizations, and engaging in simple back-and-forth interactions to help them learn the basics of conversation. Between 6 and 9 months, children enjoy making noises by banging objects, passing items between their hands, and dropping things to observe the outcome. Caregivers should understand that these activities are part of the child’s learning process. Communication involves responding to the child’s sounds and showing interest in their discoveries. Children at this age can recognize their name and enjoy hearing it, which reinforces their sense of identity. From 9 to 12 months, play becomes more exploratory, with activities like playing peek-a-boo or finding hidden objects. These games help children understand object permanence and develop problem-solving skills. Communication at this stage involves naming objects and people, teaching simple gestures like waving bye-bye, and encouraging the child to connect words with their meanings. For children aged 12 months to 2 years, play includes stacking objects, putting items into containers, and taking them out. These activities help develop fine motor skills and problem-solving abilities. Caregivers should encourage the child’s efforts to walk, play new games, and learn new skills, offering help and praise to boost the child’s confidence. Communication involves asking simple questions, responding to the child’s attempts to talk, and engaging in conversations during daily activities like feeding and bathing. For children aged 2 years and older, play activities focus on naming and counting objects, drawing, and solving simple puzzles. Caregivers can use household items to create toys that help the child learn colors, shapes, and sizes. Communication at this stage involves encouraging the child to talk, answering their questions, and teaching them stories, songs, and games. Caregivers should use kind words to soothe and praise the child, fostering a positive learning environment. Throughout all stages, caregivers should provide affection, respond to the child’s interests, and praise their efforts to learn new skills. These practices not only support the child’s development but also strengthen the bond between the caregiver and the child. By observing and understanding the child’s needs, caregivers can provide sensitive and responsive care that promotes healthy growth and development.
